The coverage comes from the `Matcher` when it implements `text.Coverer` and knows the font: fontconfig's character set (`FcPatternGetCharSet`, kept by `Config` from the `Match` that listed the font), the footprints of go-text's `fontscan` (`Footprint.Runes`), and the readings of the `androidfonts` and `winfonts` matchers (the cmap they read for `Fallback`); for every other font (a loaded or bundled font, a font of a matcher that does not know it) it comes from the `cmap` table alone, read once and kept. The control characters (general category `Cc`: the tab, `\r`, `\n`) and the default-ignorable code points (U+200B, U+200D, U+FEFF, the variation selectors, the soft hyphen) have no glyph of their own to look for: they resolve to the first face of the style that loads, with no search and no system fallback, and go-text's face splitting already lets them stay in the run of the character before them. A rune that no candidate covers goes to the system fallback, then to the first face's missing-glyph box, without parsing the others. The tab stops of 1.4 still measure with the space of the paragraph font.
- **Font queries** (1.2, M22). `PlatformDispatcher.ResolveFont(family, weight, style)` says which face a family resolves to: a `ui.ResolvedFont` with the family name of the face (which can differ from the name asked for: a generic name such as `monospace` gives the system's monospace font, an alias such as `Arial` the font it stands for), the file and the index in it (empty for a loaded or bundled font), where the font comes from (`FontOriginLoaded`, `FontOriginBundled`, `FontOriginSystem`) and its weight and slant as the font says. It is the first font of the family that loads, in the order of §10's fallback, and false for a family that has no font (it does not resolve to the default font). `PlatformDispatcher.InstalledFontFamilies()` lists the families of the system (fontconfig's `FcFontList`; without fontconfig, the families of the font scan, named as their fonts name them), the bundled and the loaded fonts, sorted without regard to case. `PlatformConfiguration` carries the desktop's font settings (`UIFontFamily`, `UIFontSize`, `MonospaceFontFamily`, `MonospaceFontSize`, in points, from GNOME's `font-name` and `monospace-font-name`, §8.8), read with `PlatformDispatcher.UIFont()` and `MonospaceFont()`. A text engine that cannot answer (`ui.FontQueryEngine`) gives false and nil.
- **Glyph outline cache** (1.2, M22). A paragraph's glyphs are drawn from cached outlines (`internal/text/layout/paint.go`); the cache keeps the most recently used 16,384 and drops the oldest when it is full, instead of clearing everything.
- **Tab stops** (1.4, M22; a Glutter addition: Flutter has none, §12.10). `ui.ParagraphStyleOpts.TabSize` is the distance between two tab stops, as a count of the advance of U+0020 SPACE in the paragraph's own font (the `FontFamily`, `FontSize`, `FontWeight` and `FontStyle` of the paragraph style, as the number of `tab-size` is in CSS); it is a `float64` and 0, the default, keeps Flutter's behavior (a tab is white space with no stop). A negative, `NaN` or infinite value panics with the tag `TabSizeInvalid`. `painting.TextPainterOpts.TabSize` (and `TextPainter.TabSize`/`SetTabSize`, `TextPainterComputeWidthOpts.TabSize`, `GetParagraphStyleOpts.TabSize`) passes it on; `Text`, `RichText`, `RenderParagraph` and `EditableText` do not have it yet. With a tab size, a tab advances to the next multiple of the tab width measured from the start of its line, as CSS's `tab-size` does; a tab that begins on a stop advances a whole tab width, never 0. The letter spacing and word spacing of the tab's style are added after the tab, as CSS does, so the next stop is measured from where the text goes on. The tab draws nothing.
  - *Start of the line.* Positions are measured in logical order from the start edge of the line: the left edge of a left-to-right paragraph, the right edge of a right-to-left one. A tab has the level of the paragraph (rule L1 of UAX #9: a segment separator takes the base level), so it is never inside a right-to-left run of a left-to-right paragraph and the text before it stays on its start side: the distance from the start edge to the tab is the sum of the advances before it, in either direction.
  - *Breaking.* A tab is a break opportunity (UAX #14 class BA, as before). A tab at the end of a line hangs, like other white space: it does not count for the width the line needs, so a line is never wrapped because of its last tab, and `LongestLine` does not include it. A wrapped line starts its tab stops again from its own start. The maximum intrinsic width follows the stops of the unwrapped lines; the minimum intrinsic width is the widest unbreakable word, as before.
  - *Queries.* The tab's advance is the advance of its glyph, so `GetBoxesForRange`, `GetPositionForOffset`, `GetGlyphInfoAt`, the caret metrics, the line metrics and the word and line boundaries all see the whole width; a caret after a tab is at the tab stop, and a justified line widens a tab like a space.
- **Shaped run cache** (1.4, M22). Shaping is the main cost of building a paragraph, and an editor builds again lines whose spans did not change, so the engine keeps the shaped glyphs of each run (a stretch of one style, one face, one direction and one script, §10's paragraph layout steps 1 and 2) between builds. The key is the text of the run, the font face, the font features, the direction, the script and the language, and, because HarfBuzz reads the text around a run, the pre-context (whether there is any, and for the scripts that join letters, the five runes before) and the post-context (for those scripts, the five runes after): two runs with the same key shape to the same glyphs. The size is not in the key, because the engine shapes at one size and scales the result; the font variations are part of the face. A hit costs a copy of the glyphs (letter and word spacing are applied after the cache). The cache belongs to the engine and, like its other caches, is used on the UI thread only; it holds at most 4,096 runs and 8 MiB of keys and glyphs, and drops the least recently used entry when either bound is passed. It is emptied when the fonts change (`LoadFontFromList`, which is also what the `SystemFontsDidChange` path follows): the engine compares the generation of its font collection. Its results equal fresh shaping (a fuzz test compares every run of random paragraphs with the pipeline as it was before the cache).
  - *Around the cache.* What the engine finds out about a text before shaping (the bidi levels, the pieces of one level and one script, the line break opportunities, the grapheme clusters and, when a query asks, the words) does not depend on the fonts or the styles, so it is kept by text, direction and language in a second least-recently-used cache (2,048 texts, 4 MiB), which fonts do not empty. Text that is all ASCII in a left-to-right paragraph, and text below U+0300 for the clusters, take shortcuts that give what go-text's segmenter gives (a test compares them on random text). The faces of the ASCII characters of a style are kept in an array, and the last eight styles that were looked up are found by their values. `ui.ParagraphBuilder` keeps one `ResolvedTextStyle` for each pushed style, and `ui.TextRun.Style` points to it.
  - *Layout on demand.* `BuildParagraph` no longer lays the paragraph out: the intrinsic widths are known at once, and anything else that asks (`Layout` for a width, or a query, or painting) finds it laid out, with an infinite width when nothing laid it out. Flutter's `ParagraphBuilder.build` does not lay out either; a caller that calls `Layout` (as `TextPainter` does) no longer pays for a layout it throws away.
- **Paragraph layout** (`internal/text`), in this order:
  1. Spans become runs, segmented by script, direction and font, with fallback.
  2. Runs are shaped.
  3. Lines are broken, honoring `softWrap`, `maxLines` and ellipsis (and, with `TabSize`, the tab stops of each line).
     *The last line with an ellipsis* (1.8.3, step 28.22). When `maxLines` is exceeded (or, with no `maxLines`, the first line that does not fit) and the paragraph has an ellipsis, the last kept line is not the word-wrapped line: it runs from its start to the next hard break or to the end of the text, and is cut at the last grapheme cluster boundary where its text and the ellipsis fit, in the middle of a word if the word is the one that does not fit, as SkParagraph does (`Hello world this i…`). The text before the ellipsis never ends inside a cluster (a combining sequence, a ligature, an emoji with ZWJ) and the white space at its end is dropped. A box narrower than the ellipsis shows the ellipsis alone. Lines before the last still break at words, and text that fits, text without an ellipsis, and a line that ends at a hard break are unchanged. The cut is by logical order, so in a right-to-left paragraph it keeps the start of the text.
  4. Each line is reordered for bidi.
  5. Text is aligned and justified, with strut, height, leading distribution, letter and word spacing.
  6. Placeholders for `WidgetSpan` are laid out.
  7. Decorations are added: underline, overline and line-through in solid/double/dotted/dashed/wavy styles, with thickness.
  8. Metrics are computed: baselines, line metrics and intrinsics.
- **Queries for editing**: boxes for a range, position for an offset, word and line boundaries, caret metrics, glyph info.
- **Text scaling** follows Flutter's `TextScaler`, including clamping.
- **Font features and variations** are passed through to shaping.


**Decided in step 28.16** (font fallback that loads only the fonts that can help; `internal/text`, `internal/text/layout`, the matchers):
- *Why a tab loaded every font.* A run of nothing but a tab (a tab span of a highlighter, an indentation-only line, a tab at the end of a row of non-ASCII text) makes go-text ask `ResolveFace('\t')`; no font has a glyph for it, so `styleFonts.ResolveFace` parsed every candidate (`font.NewFont` parses every table and every outline) before it fell back to the first face. The 62 monospace files of Emetos were 116 MB on disk and 170 MB of Go heap.
- *Lazy outlines (task 3).* go-text cannot read the outlines of a glyph the first time it is drawn without changing it: `font.NewFont` parses `glyf` (`tables.ParseGlyf` makes every glyph), `CFF ` (`cff.Parse` reads every charstring), `GSUB`/`GPOS`, `COLR`, `sbix`, `SVG ` and the rest at once, and `font.Face` has no lazy constructor. Glutter keeps the full parse of the chosen face and does not vendor or fork go-text; the saving is that a face is chosen only when it can draw something.
- *The API.* `text.Coverer` (an optional interface of a `Matcher`, like `Aliaser`): `Covers(ctx, FontFile, rune) (has, known bool)`, `known` false when the matcher cannot tell. `Collection.Covers(ctx, FontFile, rune) (bool, error)` asks the matcher for a system font, falls back to the font's own `cmap` (`readCmap`: OS/2 for the symbol-map page, `cmap`, `font.ProcessCmap`; a loaded or bundled font from its bytes, a file opened and read once), and uses the map of a font that is parsed already. `Collection.ParsedFonts` counts the fonts `load` was called for (a failed attempt included); it is for tests and benchmarks.
- *Coverage by matcher.* fontconfig: `Config.Covers(path, index, rune)` from the character sets it keeps (a reference taken with `FcCharSetCopy` when `Match` lists the font, one per file and face, released by `Close`; FcCharSet is read with `FcCharSetHasChar`); a font that no `Match` listed is unknown. `scanMatcher`: the footprint of the face (file and the low 16 bits of the index; built into a map at the first call). `androidfonts` and `winfonts`: the same cmap reading as `Fallback` (`Options.HasGlyph`, per file and index), only for the faces of the configuration or the installed list; with the default reader a file that cannot be read is unknown, so that the Collection reads it, reports `FontLoadFailed` once and skips it; with an app-supplied `HasGlyph` the answer is always known. The cache files of `winfonts` keep no coverage (`cacheVersion` stays 1): a font's map is read on the first character asked, not at the scan. The web has no system fonts (`bundledOnly`), so its fonts are bundled or loaded and use the `cmap` path.
- *Order and results.* The candidates are still tried in the order of §10; skipping a font that has no glyph cannot change the face that draws a character, except where a matcher's coverage and the font's `cmap` disagree. A matcher's `true` is never trusted alone: the face of the font is loaded and `NominalGlyph` asked, and the search goes on if it says no. Its `false` is trusted (fontconfig's set is built from the font's Unicode `cmap`; the test compares them on 20 monospace fonts of the machine). The first face is the first candidate that loads, found once per style (`firstFace`); a file that does not load is reported to `OnFontError` once for the style instead of at each character.
- *Control and ignorable characters* are `unicode.Is(unicode.Cc, r)` or `harfbuzz.IsDefaultIgnorable(r)` (U+115F, U+1160, U+3164 and U+FFA0 are not in it, as HarfBuzz decides). A font with a glyph for the tab, listed after one that has none, no longer draws the tab (Emetos's workaround, a font with a glyph for U+0009 listed first in the row, is not needed).
- *The unreadable `cmap`.* A font whose `cmap` cannot be read is skipped: the first call of `Collection.Covers` for it fails with `FontLoadFailed` (route `Collection.Covers->Collection.loadCmap->readCmap` or `…->Collection.loadCmap`), reaches `OnFontError` once, and the later calls say it has no glyph. No new tag: it is the failure of loading a font that `Face` has.
- *The memory kept.* A `cmap` read by `Covers` stays in the `Collection` (`ProcessCmap` copies the table; a few hundred KB for a CJK font, nothing for a font with a matcher's coverage); the parsed font and its outlines are not kept for a font that is never chosen.
- *Tests.* `internal/text/fonttest` writes fonts for tests from a bundled font by replacing the `cmap` table (a format 12 subtable for a list of runes, or three bytes for a table that cannot be read), so no font file is kept in the repository. Style of 60 fonts in which only the first and the last have Latin: a tab, `\r`, `\n`, DEL, a C1 control, U+200B, U+200D, U+FEFF, U+FE0F, U+00AD, an unassigned code point and U+10FFFD parse at most the first file; a Greek letter that only the third font has, a Han character of the fifth and a Cyrillic letter of the last parse only the font that has it (the brief said "the first and the third" for Greek: the first font is not parsed because no search needs it); the answer per rune is cached; a matcher that knows its fonts is believed with files that are not there; an unreadable `cmap` is reported once; the first face is the first that loads; a tab-stop paragraph measures the same over 1 and 60 fonts. Coverage of each matcher is tested against the `cmap` of the same file (fontconfig and `fontscan` against the machine's fonts, `androidfonts` and `winfonts` over their fixtures and real files).
- *Benchmark.* `BenchmarkFirstLayoutManyFonts` (`internal/text/layout/bench_fonts_test.go`; numbers in `docs/PERFORMANCE.md`, "Text: font fallback").

### 11.3 Additions in 1.2 (M22)

- **`TreeSliver`** (`widgets`, Flutter's `widgets/sliver_tree.dart`): a sliver that shows a tree of nodes as an indented list that expands and collapses (`TreeSliverNode`, `TreeSliverController`, `TreeSliverStateMixin`'s toggling, `TreeSliverIndentationType`, `TreeSliverNodeCallback`, `TreeSliverNodeBuilder`, `TreeSliverRowBuilder` and the `RenderTreeSliver` that lays the rows out). It is a code editor's file tree. Ported from `reference/flutter/packages/flutter/lib/src/widgets/sliver_tree.dart` and `rendering/sliver_tree.dart` with their tests.
- **`ReorderableListView`** (`material`, Flutter's `material/reorderable_list.dart`): the Material list whose items the user drags to reorder (`NewReorderableListView`, `NewReorderableListViewBuilder`, `buildDefaultDragHandles`, the drag handle on desktop, the proxy decorator, `header`, `footer`). It is built on `widgets.SliverReorderableList`, which exists since step 9.3; it is done in step 22.8.
- **Tab stops and the shaped run cache** (1.4, §10): `ParagraphStyleOpts.TabSize`, passed through `TextPainterOpts.TabSize`, and a cache of shaped runs in the text engine that makes a line whose spans did not change cheap to build again (`docs/PERFORMANCE.md`).

**Decided in step 28.17** (`TreeSliverNode.SetExpanded`; `widgets/sliver_tree.go`). *Where it works.* `SetExpanded` changes the field of any node, shown or not; a hidden node shows its value when its ancestors open, because the active nodes are made from the `expanded` fields. A node that is shown holds a second callback (with the one of 27.9), set when the active nodes are made; it is not called while `toggleNode` runs (the toggle makes the active nodes itself), so a `SetExpanded` of another shown node inside `OnNodeToggle` appears at the next remake, and it does nothing for a node that is not among the active nodes (hidden, removed, or in a tree that is gone). *No animation.* The tree ends the node's animation (a toggle in progress), makes the active nodes again and ends the animations of the nodes that left, in one `SetState`; the rows are at their final places in the next frame (the arrow of the default node builder is a widget with an animation of its own, `AnimatedRotation`, and still turns over the toggle duration, as it does when the node's widget is built with another value). The controller's `ExpandNode`, `CollapseNode` and `ToggleNode` animate as before. `SetExpanded` does not call `OnNodeToggle`, which is the callback of a toggle by the user or the controller. *The rule for `NodeKey`.* A tree with a `NodeKey` that is given new node objects gives each new node that has children, or is lazy, the expansion of the old node with the same key (27.9). A node on which the app called `SetExpanded` since a tree last took it in (any value, even the one the node had: the app said what it wants) is left as it is. The mark is cleared when a tree with a `NodeKey` takes the node in, so a later tree built with this node object, and an old node with the same key, carries over again. Without a `NodeKey` nothing is carried, and `SetExpanded` only sets the node's own value. An app that sets the expansion of every node from its model therefore gets its model, and one that sets only some gets the old expansion for the others. A `SetExpanded` after the node is in the tree is simply later than the carry-over and wins. The constructor's `Expanded` is not a call of `SetExpanded`: the old expansion still wins over it, as in 27.9. A node with no children that is not lazy stays collapsed, and if children come later it is still collapsed (as a leaf that is given children is in 27.9).

### 11.4 A list keeps what the user reads in place (1.9.2)

`MaintainVisibleContentPosition` (`ListViewOpts`, and the options of the constructors of `SliverList`, `SliverFixedExtentList`, `SliverVariedExtentList` and `SliverPrototypeExtentList`; not grids, not `SliverAnimatedList`) makes a list with keyed items keep the items that the user reads where they are on the screen when items are inserted before them. Flutter does not: `SliverMultiBoxAdaptorElement.performRebuild` clears the layout offset of a child that moved to a new index and gives the old offsets to the children now at the old indices, so inserting 3 rows of 50 pixels at item 0 moves a visible row by 150 pixels, with and without `findChildIndexCallback`, at offset 0 and at an offset inside the list (checked on 2026-10-27). The option is for a live log: a reverse `ListView` whose offset 0 is the newest row, where the user reads an older row while new ones arrive.

- **What counts.** The option works for the children whose element moves to a new index by its key: a builder list with `FindChildIndexCallback` (or `FindItemIndexCallback`) and a key on each item, or the keys of the children of `NewListView`. Without keys, or without a way to find them, it does nothing. Separators of a separated list have no key and stay at their index.
- **At the leading edge.** The leading edge is a sliver whose last constraints have a `ScrollOffset` of at most `foundation.PrecisionErrorTolerance` (or that has not been laid out). There the list does what Flutter does and follows the start: the new items appear at the start and the others move.
- **Away from it, `SliverList`.** `PerformRebuild` keeps the layout offset of a child that moved and does not hand the old offsets to the children that take the old indices. The indices before the lowest child that moved are not built then: they are built when the sliver scrolls to them (no row is built and thrown away). The visible children do not move and the scroll offset does not change. `RenderSliverList` already lays out leading children that have no offset. When the user scrolls to within the cache extent of the start, it inserts every child before the first one in one layout pass and corrects the scroll offset once, by their extent less the offset of the first child (`rendering.SliverVisibleContentKeeper.KeepsVisibleContentPosition`; Flutter's loop corrects one child for each pass, and a viewport allows ten passes). When the sliver itself is at offset 0 (a jump to the start) there is no correction: the list starts at its first item. So the scroll extent above the kept children is not known until the user comes near it, and a scroll bar reflects the old extent until then.
- **Away from it, the lists whose offsets come from the index** (`SliverFixedExtentList`, `SliverVariedExtentList`, `SliverPrototypeExtentList`). The element finds the first child that ends after the scroll offset, and after the rebuild it asks the render object for the layout offset of that child's new index. The difference is kept as a pending correction. The next layout of the sliver returns it as a `ScrollOffsetCorrection` before it lays out anything (`SliverVisibleContentKeeper.TakeScrollOffsetCorrection`), once, only in the frame with the insertion. The offset of the scroll controller changes by the height of the new items, and the visible items do not move. Two rebuilds before a layout give one correction (the second replaces the first, both measured from the offsets of the last layout).
- **Limits.** An insertion between the kept children (inside the cache extent before the visible items) moves the visible items below it, as in Flutter, since `SliverList` lays out from its first child. The option costs nothing when it is off.

## 12. API conventions (Flutter → Go)

### 12.1 Constructors (D1)

Every widget and every public framework class is created by a constructor function:

```go
func NewX(<required parameters...>, opts ...XOpts) *X
```

- Flutter's `required` parameters become **positional parameters**, so leaving one out is a compile error.
- Optional parameters live in `XOpts`. You can omit it entirely. Passing more than one `XOpts` value panics with tag `MultipleOptions`.
- Widgets are **immutable after construction**. Their fields are unexported and read through methods: Flutter's `widget.title` becomes `w.Title()`.
- Constructors with **more than 6 required parameters** (e.g. `ThemeData.raw` has 82, `SemanticsData` has 32) are reviewed case by case. By default they aren't public API; the friendlier constructor plus `CopyWith` is offered instead.

### 12.2 Positional order

1. Flutter's required parameters, in declaration order, **except** `child`/`children`/`sliver`/`slivers`, which always come last
2. then `opts ...XOpts`

```go
m.NewPadding(m.NewEdgeInsetsAll(8), child)
m.NewElevatedButton(s.save, m.NewText("Save"))       // onPressed, child
m.NewElevatedButton(nil, m.NewText("Save"))          // nil onPressed = disabled, as in Flutter
m.NewAnimatedContainer(300*time.Millisecond, child, m.AnimatedContainerOpts{Curve: m.Curves.EaseOut})
```

A required-but-nullable Flutter parameter (`required VoidCallback? onPressed`) is still positional. Writing `nil` is the explicit choice Flutter requires.

### 12.3 Options and defaults

- Fields have Flutter's names in Go case (`mainAxisAlignment` → `MainAxisAlignment`). The `key` parameter is the `Key` field of every `XOpts`.
- **A zero value means "Flutter's default"**. Where that isn't possible:
  - A nullable parameter whose `null` behaves differently from Go's zero value becomes `foundation.Opt[T]` (`m.Some(v)`). Examples: `Container.Width` (null = unconstrained, 0 = zero), `TextStyle.Color` (null = inherit), `Text.MaxLines`.
  - A `bool` whose Flutter default is `true` becomes `Opt[bool]` (e.g. `SoftWrap`). Names are never inverted.
  - Every enum's zero value is `<Enum>Unspecified`, which means "this widget's default". Flutter's values follow in declaration order: `MainAxisAlignmentStart`, `MainAxisAlignmentEnd`, ...
- Immutable value classes with many fields (`TextStyle`, `ThemeData`, `BoxDecoration`, `InputDecoration`, `ButtonStyle`) are passed as pointers from their constructors; `nil` means `null`. `CopyWith(XCopy)` takes a generated struct whose fields are all `Opt[T]`, so "not given" and "set to zero" stay distinguishable.
- Value types without required parameters (`Offset`, `Size`, `Rect`, `EdgeInsets`, `Alignment`, `Color`) are plain structs and may be written as literals: `m.EdgeInsets{Left: 8, Right: 8}`.

### 12.4 Naming

| Flutter | Glutter |
|---|---|
| `Text('hi')` | `m.NewText("hi")` |
| named constructor `ListView.builder(...)`, `EdgeInsets.all(8)` | `m.NewListViewBuilder(...)` returning `*ListView`; `m.NewEdgeInsetsAll(8)` |
| static method `Theme.of(context)`, `Navigator.push(context, r)`, `TextStyle.lerp(a, b, t)` | `m.ThemeOf(bc)`, `m.NavigatorPush(bc, r)`, `m.TextStyleLerp(a, b, t)` |
| `maybeOf` | `XMaybeOf(bc) (T, bool)` |
| enum `MainAxisAlignment.center` | `m.MainAxisAlignmentCenter` |
| constants `Colors.blue`, `Icons.add`, `Curves.easeIn` | read-only package values `m.Colors.Blue`, `m.Icons.Add()`, `m.Curves.EaseIn` (`Icons` is the exception: its icons are methods, see §12.10) |
| typedefs `VoidCallback`, `ValueChanged<T>`, `WidgetBuilder` | `func()`, `func(T)`, `func(bc BuildContext) Widget` with the same names as types |
| `BuildContext context` | `bc BuildContext` (`ctx` is reserved for `context.Context`) |

### 12.5 Writing your own widgets

Go embedding isn't inheritance, so the framework decides an element's kind from the **interfaces the outer type implements**. The embedded base struct carries the key and a marker:

```go
type CounterPage struct {
	m.StatefulWidget          // marker + key
	title string
}

func NewCounterPage(title string, opts ...m.WidgetOpts) *CounterPage {
	return &CounterPage{StatefulWidget: m.NewStatefulWidgetBase(opts...), title: title}
}

func (p *CounterPage) CreateState() m.State { return &counterPageState{} }

type counterPageState struct {
	m.StateOf[*CounterPage]   // Widget(), SetState, Mounted, Lifetime, Context
	count int
}

func (s *counterPageState) Build(bc m.BuildContext) m.Widget { /* ... */ }
```

- **Lifecycle hooks** are optional interfaces: `InitState()`, `DidChangeDependencies()`, `DidUpdateWidget(old W)`, `Deactivate()`, `Activate()`, `Dispose()`, `Reassemble()`. The framework does its own bookkeeping, so there's nothing like Flutter's `super.initState()` to call.
- **Mixins become embedded structs**: `m.SingleTickerProvider`, `m.TickerProvider`, `m.AutomaticKeepAliveClient`.
- **Render objects** embed `rendering.RenderBox` and call `rendering.InitRenderBox(&r.RenderBox, r)` in their constructor. That gives the base a pointer to the outer object for its "virtual" calls (`PerformLayout`, `Paint`, `HitTestChildren`, ...).
- **Inherited data** uses generics: `m.DependOn[*AppConfig](bc)` and `m.GetInherited[*AppConfig](bc)`. You don't write an `of` function.

### 12.6 Callbacks, async and goroutines

- Futures become goroutines plus `SetState`.
  - `SetState` is safe from any goroutine. On the UI thread it runs immediately, as in Flutter. Elsewhere it's queued for the UI thread. It is silently dropped if the state is no longer mounted.
  - `s.Lifetime()` is a `context.Context` cancelled at `Dispose`.
  - `s.Go(func(ctx context.Context))` starts a goroutine with that context and with panic recovery (§14.2). Prefer it to a bare `go`.
- `FutureBuilder` takes `func(ctx context.Context) (T, error)`, and `StreamBuilder` takes a `<-chan T`. Their snapshots carry `error`.
- Flutter APIs that return a `Future` take a callback or return a channel: `NavigatorPush` returns `<-chan any`, and `ShowDialog[T]` returns `<-chan T`. Each of these is listed in §12.10.

### 12.7 Generics

`Animation[T]`, `Tween[T]` (built-in lerp for `float64`, `int`, `Color`, `Offset`, `Size`, `Rect`, `EdgeInsets`, `BorderRadius`, `Alignment`, `TextStyle`, `Decoration`; any `T` with `Lerp(T, float64) T`), `ValueNotifier[T]`, `ValueKey[T]`, `GlobalKey[S]`, `StateOf[W]`, `FormField[T]`, `DropdownButton[T]`, `PopupMenuButton[T]`, `WidgetStateProperty[T]`.

### 12.8 Operators and cascades

- Operators become methods: `a.Add(b)`, `a.Sub(b)`, `a.Mul(k)`, `a.Div(k)`, `a.TruncDiv(k)`, `a.Mod(k)`, `a.Neg()`, `rect.Shift(o)`, `m.Multiply(n)`. The comparison operators of `Offset` and `Size` are `Lt`, `Le`, `Gt` and `Ge`.
  - `Offset.Scale(sx, sy)` is Flutter's `Offset.scale`, not the `*` operator; the operator is `Mul(k)`.
  - `Size - Size` is `Sub` (gives an `Offset`) and `Size - Offset` is `SubOffset` (gives a `Size`).
  - `Matrix4.Multiply(n)` returns the product `m * n` and leaves `m` alone (Dart's `*`). `MultiplyBy(n)` sets `m = m * n` (vector_math's `multiply`).
  - The statics `Offset.lerp(a, b, t)` with nullable arguments become `OffsetLerp(a, b *Offset, t) *Offset` (and `SizeLerp`, `RectLerp`, `RadiusLerp`, `RRectLerp`, `RSuperellipseLerp`); the non-null case is the method `a.Lerp(b, t)`.
- Cascades (`..`) become separate statements.

### 12.9 Debug-only checks

Flutter's `assert` checks become checks that exist only in debug builds (`foundation.DebugMode`; release builds use the build tag `glutter_release`). What happens when one fails is in §14.2.

### 12.10 Deliberate deviations (kept up to date)

| Flutter | Glutter | Why |
|---|---|---|
| hot reload | none | not possible in Go |
| `const` widgets | none; reuse package-level values | Go has no const constructors |
| `Future` APIs | goroutine/channel/callback (§12.6) | idiomatic Go |
| `widget.x` | `s.Widget().X()` | widgets have unexported fields (§12.1) |
| `Offset.fromDirection(direction, [distance = 1.0])` | `NewOffsetFromDirection(direction, distance)` | package `ui` cannot import `foundation.Opt`; pass `1` for the default |
| `~/` on `Offset`, `Size`, `Radius` throws for infinity and NaN | `TruncDiv` returns the infinity or NaN | no exceptions in Go |
| `Matrix4` is `vector_math_64` (float64) | `ui.Matrix4` has float32 storage (§7); `TransformPoint` and `TransformRect` compute in float64 from it | smaller, and what the GPU wants |
| `RSuperellipse.contains` asks Impeller's `RoundSuperellipse` | an approximation: superellipse of exponent 5 in a box 1.2924 × the radius | Impeller's geometry is not in `reference/`; revisit with the software renderer (step 2.7) |
| Flutter records a C++ `DisplayList` | `ui.DisplayList`: a list of exported `Op...` structs (`OpDrawRect`, `OpClipPath`, ...) that the renderers type-switch on; `internal/displaylist` does not exist | an `internal` package cannot hold ops that use `ui` types without an import cycle |
| `Canvas.drawRawPoints`, `drawRawAtlas` (typed-data variants) | none | Go has slices of `Offset`, `RSTransform` and `Rect` |
| `Picture.toImage` returns a `Future` | `ToImage(width, height) (*Image, error)` and `ToImageSync` (the same) | both renderers draw on the calling goroutine |
| `Canvas.clipRect(rect, doAntiAlias: true)` | `ClipRect(rect, ClipRectOpts{DoAntiAlias: ui.Ptr(false)})`; nil means true | no `foundation.Opt` in `ui` |
| the DisplayListBuilder drops draws outside the clip | every draw is recorded | the renderers clip; culling can be added without changing the API |
| `Path` wraps `SkPath` (float32 points) | `ui.Path` follows `SkPath`'s rules (injected moves, close, arcs, conic building) with float64 points | no float32 round trips; same structure |
| `Path.getBounds` | `GetBounds` is `SkPath::computeFiniteBounds`: the box of all points, control points included, and the empty rectangle if a point is not finite. `GetTightBounds` is the exact box | Flutter's behavior; the exact one is also needed |
| `Path.addRSuperellipse` asks Impeller | corners are 8 cubics per corner on the same superellipse as `RSuperellipse.Contains` | same approximation |
| `PathMetrics` is a lazy `Iterable` | `ComputeMetrics` returns a slice of all contours with a length | simpler; contours are measured when called |
| `Path.combine(operation, path1, path2)` uses Skia's pathops, which intersects the curves exactly and can fail | `PathCombine(op, path1, path2)` cuts the curves into lines, builds the planar graph of both paths (every crossing, touch and overlap is a vertex, found on a grid of a billionth of the size of the paths with welding of neighbouring cells), finds the winding numbers of both paths on each side of every edge with a ray, keeps the edges that the operation says are on the border, chains them into contours with the inside on the left (so holes turn the other way; fill type `NonZero`), and puts back the stretches of the original curves (cut at the crossings, with their ends on the vertices). The crossings of curves are exact up to a ten-thousandth of the size of the paths. It never fails: a path with a point that is not finite gives an empty result; more than 32768 lines make the tolerance coarser | a robust and simple method that works for inputs that cross themselves, overlap and touch, and keeps curves; exact curve intersection is out of scope |
| `Path.arcToPoint(clockwise: true)`, `PathMetric.extractPath(startWithMoveTo: true)` | `Clockwise *bool`, `StartWithMoveTo *bool` in the options; nil means true | no `foundation.Opt` in `ui` |
| (none) | `Path.Flatten`, `Path.Segments`/`ForEachSegment`, `GetTightBounds` | what the renderers need |
| `ColorSpace` starts at `sRGB` | `ColorSpaceSRGB` is the zero value; there is no `ColorSpaceUnspecified` | `Color` is a literal-able value type, and the zero value must be sRGB |
| `Paint` properties (`paint.color = c`) | accessors `p.Color()` / `p.SetColor(c)`; `Paint{}` is Flutter's `Paint()` | the defaults (opaque black, anti-alias on, srcOver, miter limit 4) are not Go zero values, so the fields are unexported |
| `Scene` is a native C++ layer tree | `ui.Scene` holds an immutable tree of exported `Layer` types (`ContainerLayer`, `TransformLayer`, `ClipRectLayer`, `OpacityLayer`, `PictureLayer`, ...) that the renderers type-switch on | same reason as `ui.DisplayList`; Flutter's `pushOffset` and `pushTransform` both give a `TransformLayer` here |
| `SceneBuilder.pushX(..., oldLayer: x, clipBehavior: Clip.antiAlias)` | `PushX(args, PushXOpts{OldLayer, ClipBehavior})`; `OldLayer` is the typed handle (`*OpacityEngineLayer`, ...) and the zero `ClipBehavior` is `ClipAntiAlias` | options structs (§12) |
| `SceneBuilder.addPicture` | a nil picture is ignored; `Pop` at the root is ignored; using the builder after `Build` panics with `SceneBuilderBuilt`; `Scene.ToImage` is synchronous and `NotImplemented` until step 2.10 | programmer errors follow §14 |
| Skia's AA rasterizer unions overlapping shapes exactly | `soft` accumulates signed area per pixel and folds it with the fill rule, so coverage is exact where one edge crosses a pixel and approximate where several do (the coverage of coincident edges adds up, e.g. a stroke that retraces itself) | the golden renderer needs deterministic, simple, fast coverage; the difference is below the golden tolerance for real scenes |
| `Paint.strokeWidth == 0` is a hairline | a hairline is one device pixel wide with the paint's caps and joins (no special hairline rasterizer) | simple and deterministic |
| `Image` wraps an engine texture; `decodeImageFromPixels` takes a callback | `ui.Image` holds premultiplied RGBA8 pixels shared by its clones (`Width`, `Height`, `Pixels`, `Clone`, `Dispose`); `DecodeImageFromPixels(ctx, pixels, w, h, format, opts)` returns the image, with `rgba8888` and `bgra8888` only; `NewImageFromRGBA` wraps pixels for the renderers | the software renderer needs the pixels (step 2.7 introduced the core of what the plan gives to 2.10) |
| Skia clips are rasterized per primitive | `soft` keeps a clip as a pixel rectangle plus an optional coverage mask; an anti-aliased clip multiplies coverage (so two anti-aliased edges in one pixel multiply instead of taking the exact intersection); a clip without anti-aliasing keeps the pixels whose center is inside, with a center on the edge counting as inside | simple and deterministic |
| `drawVertices` blends the vertex colors with the paint by `blendMode` | the same, with the paint (its shader at the interpolated texture coordinates, or its color) as the source and the vertex colors as the destination, then the paint's color filters and its own blend mode; triangles are not anti-aliased | Skia's behavior as documented in `Canvas.drawVertices` |
| Skia dithers gradients when asked | `soft` always dithers gradient shaders with an 8x8 ordered matrix (at most one level of 8 bits) | smooth ramps; deterministic for goldens; the GLES shaders do the same |
| `drawAtlas` colors and `blendMode` | the sprite is the source and the color the destination (so `srcIn` with a transparent white scales the sprite's alpha); the default `src` leaves the sprite as it is | Flutter's documented example |
| `Paint.shader` on `drawImage*` | ignored: the image is the source, as in Skia | the paint's alpha, color filter, invert, blend mode, filter quality and anti-alias still apply |

A picture that was recorded again is damaged where its operations reach, even if it drew the same.
